It's May 2033. Mrs Yilmaz, Elif's mother, is taking the Goethe B1 exam next week, for citizenship. Mara is helping her. They're practising Sprechen Teil 1: they have to plan a farewell party for a colleague together.
Right, the task: a colleague is retiring. We're planning a small party together. You start, Mrs Yilmaz.
All right. When do we want to have the party? I suggest we have it on Friday after work.
Friday is bad, a lot of colleagues already have plans for the weekend then. How about Thursday?
Thursday is good too. I agree. And where? At the office or in a restaurant?
I think a restaurant is too expensive. Wouldn't it be better to celebrate at the office and everyone brings something?
Good idea! I can bring börek. And what shall we give her?
Maybe a voucher? That way she can choose something herself.
Hm, a voucher is a bit impersonal. What do you think about making a photo album? With photos of all the colleagues.
That's a lovely idea. So, we agree: Thursday, at the office, everyone brings something and we give her a photo album. Who'll take care of the photos?
I'll take care of it. And you write the invitation. Agreed?
Agreed. And now, Mrs Yilmaz, quite honestly: that was perfect. If you do it like that in the exam, you'll pass with flying colours.

Warum macht Frau Yilmaz die Prüfung?

Ayşe Yilmaz was forty when she decided to apply for German citizenship. She had been living in Berlin for nineteen years. She had come at twenty-two from a small village near Kayseri, newly married, without a word of German, and in the first years she had spoken almost nothing but Turkish: with her husband, with the neighbours, with her family on the phone. Then the children came, the children learnt German at nursery, at school, and one day Ayşe realised that her own children were speaking German to each other and that she no longer understood everything. That was the day she signed up for her first German course.

That had been six years ago. Since then she had done three courses at the Volkshochschule, in the evenings, after her work at the supermarket, while her husband put the children to bed. She had passed A1 and A2. Now only B1 was missing, for naturalisation. And since Easter she had come every Tuesday evening to Mara's on the fourth floor, with a thick exercise book, a notebook full of vocabulary and a box of home-made börek, which Jakob emptied every time before the lesson was over.

The lessons at Mara's were different from the courses at the Volkshochschule. Mara didn't explain grammar. She let Ayşe tell stories: about her village, about her grandmother, who had woven carpets, about her first winter in Berlin, when she thought the sun had disappeared for ever. When Ayşe made a mistake, Mara wrote it on a slip of paper and at the end of the lesson gave her all the slips at once. “Not while you're telling a story,” Mara said. “When you're interrupted while you're telling a story, you stop telling it. An old lady on the fourth floor taught me that. She lived right here, in this flat.”

Mara understood her better than any other teacher could have. She remembered her own B1 exam in July 2027 exactly: the sleepless night before, the exam room at the Goethe-Institut with green curtains, her partner Rana, a Syrian paediatrician, with whom she had to plan a trip and who at first couldn't get a word out because of nerves. Mara had taken her hand back then, under the table, and Rana had started to speak, and in the end they had both passed. They still wrote to each other every year at Christmas.

The exam was on a Saturday in May, at the same Goethe-Institut, in the same room with the green curtains. Mara went with Ayşe to the door. Elif had come too, with a lucky charm she had drawn herself: a little paper conker with a smiling face. “So you think of the stop, Mum,” she said. “It's being opened this afternoon. And my tree is being planted. You have to finish by three. Promise?” Ayşe laughed, for the first time that morning. “I promise,” she said.

The night before, Ayşe hadn't been able to sleep. At midnight she was sitting in the kitchen going over her vocabulary, until her husband came, made her a tea and said: “You already know everything. You just don't know yet that you know.” Then he sent her to bed, the way she usually sent the children.

The other candidates were already standing outside the door, about thirty people from all corners of the world: an older man from Afghanistan with a thick dictionary under his arm, which he had to hand in straight away, two young engineers from India, a woman from Brazil who kept muttering verbs, a grandmother from Ukraine with her granddaughter, who were both taking the exam, together, on the same day. Ayşe looked at them all and suddenly felt less alone. They all had the same goal. They had all once left their village, their town, their country, and now had to prove that they had arrived here.

Lesen went well. Hören went better than she had thought; only with an announcement at the station did she not understand the platform, and she simply ticked an answer, as Mara had advised her. Schreiben was hard. The formal email to a landlord, in which she had to complain about a broken heating system, she wrote three times before it sounded right. And then came Sprechen. Her partner was a young woman from Vietnam, Linh, who worked as a cook and was so nervous that her hands were shaking. The task: to plan a trip for a German course together.

Ayşe saw the shaking hands. And she remembered the story Mara had told her, about Rana, the table and the green curtains. Very carefully, so that the examiners wouldn't see, she put her hand on Linh's hand under the table. Linh looked at her in surprise. Then she took a deep breath. And Ayşe began, slowly and clearly: “Shall we think first about where we're going? I suggest we go to a lake. What do you think?” And Linh answered, quietly at first, then more and more confidently.

They planned a trip to the Müggelsee, by train, not by bus, because Linh got sick on buses, which she explained in such perfect German that one of the examiners had to smile. They argued politely about whether to have a picnic or go to a restaurant and agreed on both: first a picnic, then ice cream. Ayşe suggested that everyone bring a dish from their own country. Linh agreed and promised spring rolls. And when the examiner said the time was up, the two women looked at each other and laughed, as if they really had planned a trip and not just taken an exam.

At half past two Ayşe came out of the exam room, with red cheeks and tired eyes. Mara was waiting for her outside on a bench, with two cups of coffee. “Well?” she asked. Ayşe sat down, took a cup and said nothing for a long time. Then she said: “I don't know if I've passed. But Linh has. That I know.” Mara looked at her and understood straight away. She hugged Ayşe, in the middle of the bench outside the Goethe-Institut, and said: “Then you've passed too. Believe me. The examiners see everything. Even under the table.”

On the way to the tram, Linh caught up with them, out of breath, with her phone number on a slip of paper. “I just wanted to thank you,” she said in German, and then, because she couldn't find the words, in English: “You saved me.” Ayşe took the slip of paper and put it in her pocket next to Elif's paper conker. “No,” she said. “We saved each other. And in the summer we'll do the trip to the Müggelsee for real. With spring rolls and börek.” Linh laughed and nodded. Mara, who was standing beside them, thought of Rana and the green curtains and of how some things repeat themselves, only a little more beautifully each time.

At three they were standing on Kastanienallee. The new stop was finished: a wide, flat platform, exactly level with the tram door, a glass roof, two benches, a digital display that announced out loud when the next tram was coming, for those who couldn't see. A red ribbon was stretched across the platform. Mrs Krause from the district office was holding a big pair of scissors. Dr Hartmann from the BVG gave a speech that nobody heard, because everyone was looking at something else: at a small hole in the ground, right next to the stop, and at a young chestnut tree, a metre tall, with seven green leaves, in a flowerpot labelled “Elif”.

Elif planted the tree herself. Her father helped her with the spade, Ludwig held the little trunk straight, and Ayşe, with the exam still in her bones, poured the water from a red watering can. Then Mrs Krause cut the red ribbon, everyone clapped, and at that very moment the first tram pulled into the new stop, the M1, a new step-free tram. The doors opened. And Ludwig got on, all by himself, without his stick, with one hand on the grab rail, for the first time in two years at his own stop. The driver, a young man with an old BVB badge on his jacket, turned round and grinned.
Leo? But you haven't finished your apprenticeship yet!

Leo laughed. “No, Grandpa. I don't start until September. I'm not driving today. Mr Wolff just let me ride along and ring the bell. For the first run from the new stop.” And then Leo rang the bell, once, loud and clear, and the real driver, an older man with a grey moustache, said over the loudspeaker: “Bitte zurückbleiben.” (“Please stand back.”) And Ludwig, who was standing at the window, saw the little tree go by, and Elif waving, and Ayşe hugging Mara, and the whole house at number thirty-one standing at the windows. Three weeks later the letter from the Goethe-Institut came. Ayşe Yilmaz had passed. Sprechen: 98 points out of 100.
